title: X Feed Digest
summary: Agent workflow is moving past one-chat-one-model usage. The strongest posts were about orchestration: long-running Codex jobs, recursive review/fix loops, and manager agents that dispatch specialists instead of making the human babysit every thread.

Model selection is starting to matter as much as model quality. Several posts converged on the same point: there is no universal winner across GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, DeepSeek V4, and Kimi K2.6, so routing by task, cost, and reliability is becoming a core skill.

Enterprise AI is getting more operational and less demo-like. Deterministic execution surfaces, persistent memory, and voice-first controls all showed up, suggesting the stack is shifting from chat novelty toward software that actually runs work.

The market read-through centered on second-order effects: the Musk/OpenAI trial could surface real governance details, AI is pushing value toward scarce chip manufacturing capacity rather than pure design labor, and geopolitics is now a live risk to frontier-AI dealmaking.

items.title: @thsottiaux: Codex Can Stay on Hard Problems for Days
items.body: An OpenAI engineer said GPT-5.5/Codex can already sustain very long-running tasks with a few workflow tweaks, and that product changes are coming to make this easier. The real signal is that durability and supervision are becoming as important as raw model IQ for coding agents.

items.title: @steipete: Recursive Codex Review Loops Are in Production
items.body: Peter Steinberger shared a workflow where Codex reviews every landed commit, opens a follow-up PR if it finds a bug, and can trigger more review/fix loops up to five times. That is a strong example of agents moving from assistant mode into continuous software-process infrastructure.

items.title: @frxiaobei: One Manager Agent Beats Chatting with Five Agents
items.body: A practical OpenClaw workflow post argued that once an agent or skill is stabilized in Codex or Claude Code, the better pattern is to hand it to a long-running manager agent and stop micromanaging every worker. The useful takeaway is that orchestration quality now matters more than spinning up yet another chat.

items.title: @ai_xiaomu: No Single Model Won This Release Week
items.body: One of the clearest model-ranking posts of the batch argued that Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, DeepSeek V4-Flash, and Kimi K2.6 each dominate different tradeoffs rather than one model winning outright. That matches where the market feels headed: routing skill is becoming a competitive advantage.

items.title: @xiaochuan8688: Musk v. Altman Matters for Disclosure More Than the Verdict
items.body: The sharpest trial commentary in the feed framed the Musk-OpenAI case as important less for Musk's odds of winning and more for what four weeks of evidence could reveal about OpenAI's governance, conversion, and valuation. For markets, that makes the courtroom a potential information event, not just a legal sideshow.

items.title: @williamlong: Meta-Manus Unwind Risk Is Now Real
items.body: A widely shared post relayed the Wall Street Journal report that Meta is preparing to unwind its Manus acquisition after Chinese regulators blocked the deal. The bigger signal is that frontier-AI M&A is now exposed to post-signing geopolitical reversal risk in a very concrete way.

items.title: @LinQingV: AI Makes Chip Design Cheaper, Not Fabrication
items.body: A strong semiconductor thread argued that AI can collapse the labor needed to design inference chips, but it does nothing to reduce the real bottlenecks: tapeout cost, advanced fabs, packaging, and HBM. That is a useful investing lens because it shifts value away from design labor and toward hard manufacturing scarcity.

items.title: @fuguizhuo: AI Raises the Value of Judgment, Not Just Speed
items.body: A good summary of Linear CEO Karri Saarinen's AI notes argued that AI makes it easier to produce both great work and garbage, which means expertise and taste matter more, not less. The especially useful nuance was that AI is strongest for exploration and variant generation, not automatically for final production design.

items.title: @wey_gu: Reliability Is a Real Multi-Model Reason
items.body: One practical post said the reason to pay for both OpenAI and Anthropic is not only capability spread but uptime insurance: if one provider or GitHub itself is flaky, work should not stop. That is a mundane point, but it is increasingly the correct one for serious AI-assisted development.

items.title: @op7418: GitHub Outages Are Creating an AI-Native Infra Opening
items.body: A thread on Ghostty's planned move off GitHub argued that repeated instability in Actions, PRs, and Issues is making the platform harder to trust for heavy development. If that sentiment spreads, there may be a genuine opening for a git host built around AI-heavy workflows instead of legacy assumptions.

items.title: @cheery9998: Use One AI to Bootstrap the Rest of Your Mac Setup
items.body: A nice workflow tip for a fresh Mac was to install the basics first, then let one coding agent install and wire up the rest of the AI toolchain across Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and a split-terminal workspace. It is simple, but it captures the current best practice: use AI first for setup and environment glue, not only for writing code.
